analysis.one_liner: Repeals about a dozen special tax breaks for oil and gas companies, making them pay more in taxes.
analysis.headline: The bill repealing oil and gas tax subsidies never left the House committee it was assigned to and never got a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would strip away a series of special tax provisions that oil and gas companies use to lower their tax bills — including deductions for drilling costs, credits for marginal wells, percentage depletion, and LIFO accounting for the biggest oil companies. It would also make tar sands and oil shale fuels subject to the petroleum excise tax. The goal is to end federal tax subsidies for fossil fuel production and raise revenue from the industry. The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and received no further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who currently bear the cost of these tax breaks through forgone federal revenue. Companies without these special breaks — including competitors in other energy sectors — would face a more even tax playing field.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the deduction for intangible drilling and development costs, which lets oil and gas producers write off drilling expenses immediately rather than over time [S2][S3].
Repeals percentage depletion, a deduction that allows oil and gas producers to deduct a set percentage of gross income from wells [S2][S3].
Repeals tax credits for producing oil from marginal wells and for enhanced oil recovery, and the deduction for tertiary injectant expenses [S2][S3].

Bars major integrated oil companies (those producing at least 500,000 barrels a day with over $1 billion in receipts) from using last-in, first-out accounting, which lowers their reported taxable income [S2][S3].

Limits foreign tax credits for dual capacity taxpayers — companies that pay levies to foreign governments and receive specific economic benefits in return — and expands the crude oil excise tax to cover tar sands and oil shale fuels [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies of all sizes, from major integrated producers to small operators of marginal wells, who would lose deductions and credits and pay more tax. Some of the added cost could eventually show up in fuel prices, though the biggest provisions target the largest companies.

drawbacks.text: Removing drilling-cost deductions, depletion, and marginal-well credits raises the cost of producing oil and gas, which critics argue would reduce domestic production and put some upward pressure on fuel prices for consumers [S2].

Small operators would be hit hard: the credits for marginal wells and enhanced oil recovery largely benefit smaller and stripper-well producers, and ending the passive loss exception would discourage individual investment in drilling ventures [S2][S3].
The bill is a revenue-raising tax change with no offsetting relief for consumers, so any energy cost increase would land on households alongside the industry [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits are straightforward: ending special-purpose tax breaks raises federal revenue and ends preferential treatment for one industry. The costs are real but narrower — some upward pressure on production costs and fuel prices, with disproportionate effects on small marginal-well operators. On balance it is a well-targeted repeal of industry-specific tax provisions rather than a broad energy tax, though honest supporters should acknowledge the price-pressure risk in an industry that ultimately passes costs to consumers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced in March 2023, the committee never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Earl Blumenauer introduced the bill on March 9, 2023, joined by Reps. Casten and Porter, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S1][S3][S5].
Seventeen House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did [S4].
The Ways and Means Committee never held a markup or reported the bill, and it never received a floor vote in the House [S5].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, with the bill still sitting in committee [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies keep the full set of special tax deductions and credits the bill would have repealed, and taxpayers continue to bear the forgone revenue.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 17 cosponsors were Democrats, with no Republican support, and the Republican-run Ways and Means Committee never took the bill up [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would repeal roughly a dozen deductions, credits, and accounting methods the industry uses to cut its tax bill, including percentage depletion, immediate expensing of drilling costs, and marginal-well credits. Keeping those breaks means taxpayers forgo the revenue [S2][S3].
The largest producers (500,000+ barrels a day, over $1 billion in receipts) would be barred from LIFO inventory accounting, which typically lowers reported income and taxes [S3].

industries.industry: Tar sands and oil shale producers
industries.note: Fuels derived from bitumen and kerogen-bearing sources would become subject to the petroleum excise tax, closing what the bill treats as a gap in the tax on crude oil [S2][S3].
